speechtext:
I feel almost at a loss, Mr. Speaker, to find something to talk about this afternoon in view of the fact that so many subjects have been discussed up to the present time. Being one of the 262 members of the house, however, I feel that I must have my little say also.
Before going on to my main subject I should like to associate myself with the impassioned plea made some days ago by the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) when he asked the government to fulfil their promises with regard to the building of a railroad line to fill the gap between Heinsburg and Frenchman s Butte, and also the Bonnyville line. While neither of those branches is in my constituency, Heinsburg is just across the north Saskatchewan river and many of the people in my constituency are obliged to go there in order to market their products. With the support of the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Decore), the hon. member for Meadow Lake (Mr. Harrison), and the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene), I am sure that we should finally get some action in having those gaps completed. The government made promises years ago and many elections have gone by since that time; those

The Budget-Mr. Fair
promises have been reiterated time and again. Let us hope that they will soon be made good.
While speaking of railroad lines I should also like to mention, for the benefit of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), another railroad in the southern end of my constituency and in the northern part of the constituency of Acadia; that is the Bulwark northeasterly railroad. On many occasions the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) and I have visited the minister in connection with this line and so far we have not found any rails laid. I may say that some years ago the grade of that particular branch was built, but so far no rails have been laid and no trains are running. I hope that in this case also some action will soon be taken.
Yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) made a speech on a subject that I believe is of interest to everybody in Canada today; I refer to oil. Some people might say that I am actually soaked in oil, but that is not quite correct, although I have oil over practically all of my constituency. One of the places mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary West yesterday, Lloydminster, is of particular interest to me because I landed there on January 10, 1914; and in getting out of town to go out on a farm I almost froze to death. Since that time we have developed quite a thriving oil industry there instead of being dependent on farming as the sole industry. We have several wells producing there, but I am sorry to say, because of conditions over which the companies operating there have no control, they are not able to take all of the available supply of oil out of those wells. Some relief was given to those companies recently by the removal of the eight per cent sales tax on oil for heating purposes. The Lloydminster people and I greatly appreciate the action of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the government in removing that eight per cent sales tax. But there is one other item that we should like to see removed also; that is the exorbitant freight rates that those people are obliged to pay on the output of those wells. If something is done to meet their requests-and I believe the government feels that it should be done and I hope in the near future it will be done-then the Lloydminster field will be in a much better position to contribute something really worth while to Canada. If this problem is taken care of- that is, if the discriminatory freight rates is removed-then in the Lloydminster district we shall be able to supply quite a good deal of the oil that is now being supplied by importations from the United States. I hope [Mr. Fair.)
therefore that in the near future-perhaps in this budget or soon after it is adopted-something will be done.
Another item of interest in my part of the country is that rumour that the C.B.C. are going to have the receiving licence fees increased. I understand that they have made representations to have the fee doubled. Already I have received dozens of letters as well as resolutions from boards of trade all over my constituency vigorously protesting against any such increase. At the present time many people feel that they are not getting value for their money. In some cases the complaints are over programs presented and in others they are not getting good reception. Therefore, we feel that the licence fees are already too high and there is no need to have them increased any further. Not so long ago the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) suggested that the fees be cut out altogether and that money for Canadian Broadcasting Corporation purposes be taken out of the federal treasury. Perhaps that would be a much better way to finance the organization. Perhaps some paring down of expenses would also help out in that regard.
The question of aid to education has also been discussed. For many years on different occasions I have brought this matter to the attention of the house, but up to the present time little action has been taken along that line. I am quite satisfied that the people in general do not appreciate the importance of education and of the teaching profession in formulating constructive rather than destructive ideas in the human mind. I am quite satisfied that the schools of today could do much more to bring about peace in the world in the future than any of the big world-wide organizations that are operating at the present time. If we train our young people properly -when I say "properly" I mean teaching them to be true to their country, true to real Christian ideals and to many other ideals along that line-we shall not have the trouble in the future that we have had in the past of trying to avoid wars.
The destinies of the nations of the world are being determined in the classrooms of this and other countries to a far greater extent than they are being formulated in our parliaments or in other world organizations. It is our duty to see first of all that proper schools are provided and then proper equipment in the schools, and last of all that we have teachers who are a credit to our democratic system. In some of our schools and universities we find that the teaching given there is not all in the interest of our democratic way of life. Every care should be taken to see to it that the proper kind of teachers and

professors are placed in charge of those schools. I am well aware that the supply of money has a lot to do with providing these things. I am also well aware that the present method of taxation is not sufficient to take care of all the needs of education. As I, and this group, have advocated on many occasions, federal aid should be forthcoming to the provinces for the purpose of education. By that I do not mean that the federal government should take over the control of the running of the schools or anything of that kind. That is a provincial responsibility. The grants provided to the provinces should be given without strings attached so that they can be administered in the best interest of education in the provinces.
Let me turn to the matter of old age pensions. I feel that we are not doing our job properly in this regard. The matter of old age pensions comes under the heading of welfare. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is not in his seat today. I understand he is looking after other duties. He seems to be proud of the system we have. In the Ottawa Citizen of October 26, 1949, there appears a Canadian Press dispatch from New York as follows:
Canada's Health Minister, Paul Martin, said last night, healthy nations like Canada and the United States should give help and ideas to countries less advanced in their health plans.
Canada, he said, in an address prepared for delivery to the American public health association, is determined not to permit "lack of money to lead to neglect of health."
I would call special attention to this lack of money.
I was very glad to read that statement of the minister because in the administration of the department we find that the lack of money has a lot to do with citizens being denied services to which they are properly entitled.
Further on he said:
We are determined to keep abreast of the advances of medical science and to be impatient and intolerant of anything that debars our people from the best of health care.
A federal survey near the end of the war showed that Canadians were "one of the healthiest peoples in the world . . . But we also found some health statistics that gave us little cause for pride."
I might call the minister's attention to figures that were presented to the house by the then minister of national war services, Mr. LaFleche, which showed that out of 93,000 men who were examined for service in the air force and air crew only 15,000 were able to qualify. In my opinion, that is not the kind of health standard that we should have in a country like Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Fair
I am very sorry that up to the present time the government has not seen fit to increase the old age pension to at least $50 a month. That can be done. The old age pensioners of today are the senior citizens. They are the ones who have been most active in building up Canada. It is quite true that an amendment was passed last year which improved things a little; but because the government neglected, possibly deliberately, to increase the income ceiling many of the old age pensioners of today are unable to take advantage of that legislation. Many of them have been sadly disappointed when they found that the increase in the pension was absolutely of no use to them.
There is another matter to which attention should be given before this session closes. I refer to people who are unable to provide proof of age. Some other method, perhaps an examination by medical doctors or some other system, might be used so that these people are not denied their pension, as many of them are at the present time. During my years in the house I have found that several people, mainly European by birth or extraction, who came to Canada some years ago, were unable to find any record whatever of their age. Apparently births were not registered in those countries in those days. When we tried to search the records of the shipping companies or the bureau of statistics census records and so forth we were unable to find any trace of these people. Perhaps the spelling of those names, or something of that kind, may be responsible. There is no earthly reason why some method should not be devised so that these people can get the pension to which they are properly entitled. They are Canadians now. They came to Canada and did their share to build up this country, and something should be done before this session closes to see that a method is found to deal with them.
I now come to the recipients of war veterans' allowances. I think we should see to it that these men and their wives get the treatment that was recommended for them by the veterans committee and others last year. That is also denied to these people. As suggested in the case of the old age pensioners, the ceiling on income should also be increased. At the present time the amount is $1,100 a year. If any of us here were to place ourselves in the position of these burnt-out veterans we would very soon take the proper means to make available the full amount of the pension. In my opinion the amount provided is certainly not sufficient.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) who is a great humanitarian and

The Budget-Mr. Fair
always trying to do his best-even though he sometimes supports a government program which is not in the best interests of the people of Canada-made a plea to have the sales tax removed from hearing aids, and other equipment of that type. I support the hon. member in his request. I feel, too, that every support should be given to the plea made today to break up all monopolies and cartels existing in this country-because many people are denied the right to purchase many of the dentures and optical goods and other things required by them, simply because prices are too high.
There is one other class of people I shall not forget, namely those who are crippled with arthritis, infantile paralysis or any of the other dreaded ailments. Many of us who have full use of our limbs and our faculties find it difficult, under conditions over which we have no control, to make a living. When we think of these other people who in many instances are crippled and unable to help themselves, we must realize it is the duty of all Canadians to be their brothers' keeper. Canada can provide that help, and before the session closes I trust that something along this line may be done.
I come now to the subject of agriculture, and do so because it is the subject about which most people seem to have forgotten. I do not believe the consumers in Canada appreciate the work done by our farmers in this and every other country. The work of a farmer is a seven-day job, and with long hours during certain seasons of the year. He works for poorer pay than those in any other occupational group in the country.
Many farmers have less accommodation, poorer homes, less bathtubs, less telephones and less of the many other comforts of life than many other people making a good living out of the products of the farmers' labour. During the election campaign we heard of the good things the government was doing for the farmers of Canada. Perhaps we should have been told of some of the things the government was not doing for the people, in which event a different view might have been taken with respect to the government's agricultural policy.
Agriculture has been discussed in the house on many occasions, and it is my intention today to continue that discussion, because I believe that until Canada has a healthy agricultural industry we shall not have the prosperity throughout the country to which we are entitled. Many observations might be made about agriculture, but before proceeding further may I state that the farmers have on their side the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).
In the Ottawa Journal of February 10 we find a report headed "War Sacrifices of Farmers Entitle them to Fair Prices", and stating-
Canadian farmers were "entitled now" to prices which would justify their wartime sacrifices, agricultural minister Gardiner said last night. He was speaking to the annual meeting of the Ontario concentrated milk producers association at the Chateau Laurier. More than one hundred and fifty delegates are attending the two-day session, the largest in several years.
Because there have been declines in the United States, people here are suggesting that food prices should drop to that level, forgetting that prices there rose during the war to a peak never experienced here. The whole idea in preventing high food prices in Canada during wartime was to allow a "levelling out" afterwards, Mr. Gardiner remarked. He was "inclined to agree" with the popular statement that consumers did not appreciate what farmers did during the war in keeping the cost of food down.
Mr. Gardiner said he was "surprised that farmers had not been able to sell that idea fully."
I would suggest to the many new members from both rural and urban constituencies that they do their best to bring about better conditions for agriculture in Canada in the future. Agriculture has never enjoyed that prosperity to which it is properly entitled. Let us get busy, even at this late date, to improve that situation. The article continues:
People are inclined to forget that farmers, and dairy farmers in particular, were asked to hold their hand on prices during the war-at a time when they might have charged almost what they wanted.
That is the opinion of the Minister of Agriculture; and I am satisfied that if he did not have so many opponents around the cabinet council table we would have much better conditions for agriculture in Canada. Indirectly, we would have better conditions for Canadians as a whole.
The question of wheat has not been discussed in the house for some time. While some may get tired of listening to discussions concerning wheat, and the losses borne by farmers in this connection, I have not yet noticed any of those people refusing to eat either white or brown bread. It must be remembered that all of that comes from wheat, and that the farmers are required to grow that wheat.
In this connection I feel that the farmers in the prairie provinces-because they are the only ones affected-have taken a trimming which the people of Canada do not realize. For a few moments I shall deal with the British wheat agreement. I do not want anyone now or at any other time to suggest that Social Crediters are opposed to that agreement. We favoured it right from the start. It was our belief that we owed a moral obligation to Britain, and we were not slow in making our stand known. At the same time however we did make it clear that because this was a gift of the people of

Canada to the people of Britain, through the government, then the people of Canada as a whole should stand any losses suffered by the farmers in delivering wheat under this contract.
Many people feel that farmers have received much more than that to which they are entitled. Both last session and this one I have made inquiries, and through the order paper of the House of Commons I have secured certain information which I shall now place on record, in order that there shall not be any attempt to contradict or misrepresent the figures I am giving. I am satisfied these figures are authentic, and anyone wishing to check them may do so by looking up the records of the house. That should be sufficient proof.
These figures deal with losses suffered by farmers under the British wheat agreement during the first three years of operation. During the year 1946-47 the Canadian wheat board on behalf of the government delivered to Britain 169 million bushels at a price of $1.55. At the same time the wheat board sold what is known as class II wheat at an average price during that year of $2.41 a bushel. This means that up to the present time the Canadian farmer has taken a loss of 86 cents a bushel on the wheat delivered to Britain in that crop year. Let me make it clear that the $2.41, and other prices which I shall quote on class II wheat, are average prices for the average grade, while the price I am quoting for Britain will be that of No. 1 northern. That should be understood because I am making a conservative estimate of the losses. The loss on wheat delivered to Great Britain that first year amounted to $145,340,000.
During the second year of 1947-48 a total of 170-6 million bushels were delivered at a price of $1.55. The price of class II wheat for that year was $2.77. Just figuring on the basis of the 170 million bushels and leaving off the 600 thousand, at $1.22 per bushel we find that the farmers took a trimming to the extent of $207,400,000. For the third year of 1948-49 we delivered 146,142,802 bushels at a price of $2. During that year class II wheat sold at $2.22, so we have another actual loss of 22 cents per bushel amounting to $32,195,416. During the first three years of the wheat agreement the total losses amounted to $384,935,460.
We are not complaining about that, but we shall complain plenty unless those losses are made up from the federal treasury. There was no other occupational group in Canada which had their production confiscated at a price set by the government. Other operations were paid for on the basis of cost-plus or
The Budget-Mr. Fair
something of that kind, and their production was sold in most cases at prices that were not set by the government.
I intend to discuss now the wheat delivered to Canadian millers for consumption within Canada, which went on for many years prior to the period I intend to deal with. During the crop year 1946-47, 29,041,927 bushels of wheat were delivered to millers in Canada at $1.25. The price of class II wheat at that time was $2.41 per bushel. Our farmers lost $1.16 per bushel on those deliveries or a total of $33,688,635. In the latter part of that year there was an increase in the initial payment to the farmers, and in that period there was delivered to the millers for consumption in Canada a total of 24,573,939 bushels at a price of $1.55. The price of class II wheat during that period was $2.41 so that we suffered a loss of 86 cents per bushel or a total of $21,133,587.
In the crop year 1947-48 we delivered to millers in Canada 49,342,532 bushels at a price of $1.55. Class II wheat was selling at $2.77 per bushel so we accepted a loss of $1.22 or a total of $60,197,889. In the 1948-49 crop year we delivered to millers for consumption in Canada 39,281,098 bushels at a price of $2. Class II price during that period was $2.22 so therefore we lost 22 cents per bushel or a total of $8,641,841.
The total losses on wheat delivered to Canadian millers for consumption within Canada amounted to $123,661,952. When this amount is added to the amount of losses suffered under the British wheat agreement we have a total loss of $508,597,368 up to the end of the 1948-49 crop year. If anyone wishes to check these figures he will find that they have been furnished in a return made in this house.
We have been told that the farmers suffered practically no losses, but I think half a billion dollars is quite an amount for the farmers of the prairie provinces to take as a loss. That is not a very happy story for the farmers of Canada and I am one of those who delivered several thousand bushels to the pool. I know my costs of production and I know of the losses that I suffered on those deliveries.
In addition to these losses it must be remembered that ceiling prices were placed on our coarse grains at a lower figure than could have been obtained outside the country. It must also be remembered that the hogs and cattle that were fed those coarse grains were delivered on the basis of the prices fixed for wheat under the British agreement. I shall not attempt to estimate the losses suffered by our farmers in that connection, because I do not know how they could be arrived at. But if we could make an estimate I am sure it would make the farmers still more unhappy.

The Budget-Mr. Fair
On many occasions I have asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner)- on the last day of last session I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent)-whether the government was going to make these losses good, but up to the present I have not received a reply. Before this session ends I hope we shall have some indication from the government as to what they intend to do about these direct losses suffered by the farmers.
Our farmers suffered further losses because they were not permitted to ship their cattle to the United States market until a few months ago. There again I am not going to try to estimate their losses because I do not know just how they could be arrived at. We have heard a lot about the loss of markets and many people deny that such a thing exists. The Minister of Agriculture was in London last December when he had quite a bit to say about the products that we could sell except for their inability to find the dollars with which to buy them. I have a rather long quotation here which I had intended to use but time will not permit. However, I think I should quote at least a portion of it. Canada's Weekly of December 24, 1948, reports a speech made to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in London by the Minister of Agriculture as follows:
They are taking 140 million bushels of wheat and 50 million pounds of cheese from us because they must have them and we appear willing to provide them for fewer dollars than any other will supply them.
All this is bringing me to wonder if an unknown economist, or was it an Abraham Lincoln or some such individual as Churchill, was not right when he said that he would rather have the money in his pocket tied to the unthinking inanimate substance called gold which cannot change its mind than to the manipulations of some small group of crackpots who fancy themselves as economists or statesmen.
I am glad to note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is in the house. I am quite sure that when the Minister of Agriculture was referring to crackpots he was referring to the experts and advisers in the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada. Those crackpots were advised away back in December, 1945, what the results of their iniquitous legislation would be, but that went through with the support of practically everybody in the house except Social Crediters. Today they are wallowing in the mire that they created themselves. Therefore it is no wonder that conditions are as they are when there is so much manipulation for the gain of those who

control the monetary system of our country. A little further on the minister had this to
say:
X am not convinced that this latter statement is correct-
He is dealing with a statement made by one of the members of the British parliament in connection with the Marshall plan creating more communists in Europe.
-but I am convinced that the world is not in any state of mind where it can be expected to agree that the manipulation of any system or systems of currency is going to be allowed to interfere with the will of those who have empty stomachs when it is preventing surpluses of food to get to them. It might be a good thing for everybody if they would close down the United Nations meetings long enough to permit of the United Kingdom and United States experts getting together and settling some basis upon which dollars and sterling can be converted to allow nations like Canada to produce food to feed the starving millions and distribute it.
In that regard I would recommend to any who are interested in this subject the wonderful speech delivered last night by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). There is more food for thought in it than all the great world conferences provide in a whole day's proceedings. I see that my time is passing by, and I shall not be able to say everything I wanted to say. Before going further I want to point out that Canada has been a rather faithful follower of the United States in many ways. In yesterday's Ottawa Citizen there is an Associated Press dispatch from Washington. The heading is:
Truman Signs Long-Range Farm Measure
The article reads:
President Truman yesterday signed long-range farm legislation which permits the United States government to support prices of most products at or near wartime levels. The measure, passed by the present democratic congress, replaces most major provisions of the so-called Aiken law enacted by the Republican 80th congress. The Aiken law permitted somewhat lower supports for major crops.
The new law gives the secretary of agriculture authority to support virtually every farm product at 90 per cent of parity if he thinks that is advisable. Truman and agriculture secretary Brannan have indicated they favour 90 per cent supports, as a general rule, to keep agriculture prosperous.
That is what the United States intends to do for its farmers. Will Canada follow the lead taken by the United States? What are we doing here for the future? Even though the farmers of Canada have paid a very expensive premium for crop and price insurance in the future, what has the present government provided? I find that we have provided the Agricultural Prices Support Act, which will expire at the end of March, 1950, unless the legislation is renewed. There is the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which does not operate yet to the satisfaction of many

of our farmers. I do not think it even operates to the satisfaction of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). There is also the international wheat agreement. In my opinion, the government will have to go much farther than any of those measures. During the past ten years, as I said before, we have been contributing to an insurance fund for the preservation of our industry. During the next ten years we should at least get the benefits we have paid for in full in the past, by way of assured markets and guaranteed prices.
If people are of the opinion that the farmers of Canada are more prosperous than they should be, I ask them to investigate present conditions on many of our farms. They will find that, while the farmers have paid off quite a percentage of their debt in the form of mortgages and so forth, the farms are in a run-down condition, and also in many cases the machinery and other equipment. You cannot tell exactly what a farmer's financial standing is by looking at his mortgage debt because there are many other factors that should be taken into consideration. I feel it is the duty of the government to keep our basic industry prosperous. They may say again that they cannot find the money, but if that difficulty should present itself then social credit will provide the answer. Social credit has provided a reply to any argument that has been put forward in the house by any of the former ministers of finance.

speechtext: And the present one, too.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If they want a solution I am sure there are men in the Social Credit group who are familiar with the money question, and who can give them an answer, thereby contributing to the creation of a more prosperous Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to take the same privilege as most other hon. members have taken, under the latitude allowed members speaking on the budget, of bringing conditions in my own constituency to the attention of the house, hoping thereby that remedies will be provided in the near future. First of all I should like to register my approval and support of the amendment to the amendment which is to the effect that immediate consideration should be given to a reduction of tariffs sufficient to encourage an increase in imports from the United Kingdom and other sterling countries.
You will notice that the amendment to the amendment does not mention any given commodity, and I am glad of that for reasons that I shall explain later. It is quite possible that a wholesale indiscriminate reduction of tariffs would upset our economy. I understand that the trade unions have already
The Budget-Mr. Jones brought to the attention of the government the dangers involved in an indiscriminate removal of tariffs in that it could quite well upset our domestic economy with the result that there would be unemployment and chaos, and it might be followed by bankrupt factories. That is why we emphasize in our approach to tariffs and controls the need for the government to establish an import and export board whose purpose would be to encourage imports from the United Kingdom and other sterling countries, and at the same time keep a protective eye on our own domestic production so that the chaos anticipated by some of the trade unions would not take place.
Among other duties, the board would advise the government which goods could be imported, and naturally which could not be imported. They would advise as to the amount of tariff necessary to maintain the rigid control that would protect our own industries. They would advise as to the amount of the tariff, and also on what commodity it should be levied. At the same time they would keep a careful check to see that no hardship would be suffered by workers or industries in Canada. In other words, their duty would be to maintain a balance between imports and exports, plus a balance between the countries that benefit by our import and export trade. For instance, unfortunately as far as England is concerned, there is a variation between ourselves and the United States. We are taking far more from the United States than they are taking from us, and we have the reverse position in our trade with Great Britain.
It will be the duty of the board to try to balance that situation, and in that balancing to try to bring about better relations between Canada and the countries in the sterling area. It would also call for a great deal of switching of trade relations that have been carried on for many centuries. Some people will object to that, but in the last two or three years we have broken such relations with some of the English firms that have been dealing with Canada for a long time. I particularly mention those firms in Lancashire making shirtings, who shipped for many years to the shirt factories of Ontario. Last year I was talking to one manufacturer in Manchester who informed me they had not shipped a single yard of shirting to Canada-not, as one hon. member said yesterday, because the shirting trade in Canada is having its own difficulties, but because of the unfair competition of shirtings imported from the United States at prices lower than either Canada or the United Kingdom can produce this material.

The Budget-Mr. Jones

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now that the pound has been devalued has not that condition corrected itself?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Unfortunately not; we still have not re-established that trade. Devaluation should make it easier, but so far Canadian importers have not taken advantage of that situation, according to a recent letter I had from that firm.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But it is on its way.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It may come; but I am satisfied that the setting up of an import-export board would prevent that situation from again becoming top-heavy. Now with devaluation of the pound we may go to the other extreme and upset the balance of trade which would control the situation. From my personal knowledge the United Kingdom needs our exports. They need our wheat, just as they need almost everything we can produce. Contrary to the opinion held by many people, the plight in which Great Britain finds herself today is not due to the Labour government but entirely to conditions following the war. I tried to discover any way in which any other government could have improved the present position in England, and from all sides I was given the same answer, that this could not be helped, that it was inevitable and they had to suffer as a result.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You must have been speaking to your socialist friends.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I did not stay with the socialists all the time I was there. Looking at it from that point of view, we must realize that the war was not Britain's war. She was truly in the centre of it, but it was a war for civilization, and a war with a tremendous price. I sometimes wonder if payment of that price has been fairly divided among the nations who took part in the war. In other words, I believe we all have a moral responsibility, for the collapse of Britain would not only bring about the collapse of the main part of Europe but seriously upset the United States and particularly Canada.

It was stated in this house recently that someone in the United Kingdom had said she was looking to other sources to purchase wheat, particularly in the sterling areas. In the Ottawa Citizen of November 2, which is today, I read this dispatch:
The Daily Telegraph says today that Britain will discontinue purchases of Canadian newsprint next year and may cut imports of Canadian bacon and eggs by 25 per cent.
The newspaper reports that two Canadian representatives were "shocked at the severity of the cuts proposed" when they conferred with British officials last week. The Canadians were J. G. Taggart, deputy agriculture minister, and Max Mackenzie deputy trade and commerce minister.
The Telegraph says that timber imports from Canada also may be pruned.
"The decision to allocate no money for newsprint was influenced by the fact that alternative supplies are available within the sterling area," the Telegraph says. The chief alternative source is Scandinavia.
I mention that not as a warning but to show the need for immediate improvement in our trade relations with the United Kingdom before they establish themselves in other world markets and we lose that trade for good.
On motion of Mr. Jones the debate was adj ourned.
